Affine modifications and affine hypersurfaces with a very transitive automorphism group

Sh.  Kaliman ††thanks: Partially supported by the NSA grant MDA904-96-01-0012.    M.  Zaidenberg
Abstract

We study a kind of modification of an affine domain which produces another affine domain. First appeared in passing in the basic paper of O. Zariski [Zar], it was further considered by E.D. Davis [Da]. In [Ka 1] its geometric counterpart was applied to construct contractible smooth affine varieties non-isomorphic to Euclidean spaces. Here we provide certain conditions (more general then those in [Ka 1]) which guarantee preservation of the topology under a modification.

As an application, we show that the group of biregular automorphisms of the affine hypersurface X⊂𝐂k+2X\subset{\bf C}^{k+2} given by the equation u​v=p⁡(x1,…,xk)uv=p(x_{1},\dots,x_{k}) where p∈𝐂⁡[x1,…,xk],p\in{\bf C}[x_{1},\dots,x_{k}], acts m−m-transitively on the smooth part regX\,X of XX for any m∈𝐍.m\in{\bf N}. We present examples of such hypersurfaces diffeomorphic to Euclidean spaces.

Introduction

It is well known (and elementary) that for n>1n>1 the automorphism group Aut𝐂n\,{\bf C}^{n} of the affine space 𝐂n{\bf C}^{n} (or, which is the same, of the polynomial ring in nn variables 𝐂[n]:=𝐂⁡[x1,…,xn]{\bf C}^{[n]}:={\bf C}[x_{1},\dots,x_{n}]) acts m−m-transitively on 𝐂n{\bf C}^{n} for any m∈𝐍.m\in{\bf N}. That is, the diagonal action of the group Aut𝐂n\,{\bf C}^{n} on the m−m-th symmetric power Sm​𝐂n,S^{m}{\bf C}^{n}, and even on the m−m-th Cartesian power (𝐂n)m,({\bf C}^{n})^{m}, is transitive outside of the diagonals for any11 1 See [RoRu] for an ∞−\infty-transitivity property of the group of analytic automorphisms of 𝐂n.{\bf C}^{n}. m∈𝐍.m\in{\bf N}. Clearly, every Zariski open subset of the form 𝐂n∖K{\bf C}^{n}\setminus K where K⊂𝐂nK\subset{\bf C}^{n} is a finite set of points, possesses this property.

Let VV be a compact complex space. By a generalized Bochner-Montgomery Theorem [Akh, (2.3)], the automorphism group AutV\,V is a complex Lie group. Therefore, it cannot be m−m-transitive on VV for m>m>dim AutV.\,V. Thus, the question arises:

For which complex manifolds or, at least, for which quasi-projective varieties XX the group AutX\,X is m−m-transitive on XX for any m∈𝐍​?m\in{\bf N}?

Or, more restrictively (to exclude the above examples of type 𝐂n∖K{\bf C}^{n}\setminus K)

Which affine algebraic varieties possess this property?

In sections 4 and 5 we describe a class of affine hypersurfaces non-homeomorphic, in general, to the affine spaces, with very transitive automorphism groups (see The Transitivity Theorem in sect. 5).

One more remark is in order. One might specify the above problem by asking whether, for mm given, there exists an m−m-transitive algebraic group action on X.X. For mm sufficiently large with respect to the dimension of X,X, the class of such varieties XX seems to be rather poor. Actually, already the affine plane 𝐂2{\bf C}^{2} does not admit an m−m-transitive algebraic group action for m≥3.m\geq 3. Indeed, by the Jung-van der Kulk Theorem [Ju, vdK], the group Aut𝐂2\,{\bf C}^{2} can be represented as the amalgamated product of the affine group Aff𝐂2\,{\bf C}^{2} and the Jonquière subgroup J⁡(𝐂2)⊂J({\bf C}^{2})\subset Aut𝐂2\,{\bf C}^{2} of the triangular transformations (x,y)⟼(x,y+p⁡(x))(x,\,y)\longmapsto(x,\,y+p(x)) where p∈𝐂⁡[x].p\in{\bf C}[x]. By the theorem of Serre [Se], any subgroup of finite length G⊂G\subsetAut𝐂2\,{\bf C}^{2} is conjugate either with a subgroup of Aff𝐂2\,{\bf C}^{2} or with a subgroup of J⁡(𝐂2).J({\bf C}^{2}). Since the polynomial xx is an invariant of the Jonquière subgroup J⁡(𝐂2),J({\bf C}^{2}), in the latter case GG possesses a non-constant invariant function, and therefore, it is not even transitive on 𝐂2.{\bf C}^{2}. In the former case, GG is at most 2−2-transitive; indeed, the collinearity of a triple of points is preserved by the action of the affine group Aff𝐂2.\,{\bf C}^{2}. It remains to observe following D. Wright [Wr 1] that any algebraic subgroup G⊂G\subsetAut𝐂2\,{\bf C}^{2} is of finite length.

The proof of Theorem 5 on ∞−\infty-transitivity of the automorphism group of a smooth hypersurface X⊂𝐂k+2,k≥2,X\subset{\bf C}^{k+2},\,\,k\geq 2, given by the equation u​v−p⁡(x¯)=0uv-p({\overline{x}})=0 goes as follows. This hypersurface XX can be naturally presented in two different ways as an affine modification of 𝐂k+1{\bf C}^{k+1} (see below). Due to Corollary 2, one can lift to XX those automorphisms of the affine space 𝐂k+1{\bf C}^{k+1} which preserve the locus of at least one of these modifications. In such a way we obtain two subgroups G^1{\widehat{G}}_{1} and G^2{\widehat{G}}_{2} of the automorphism group AutX.\,X. It turns out that the subgroup G^{\widehat{G}} of AutX\,X generated by G^1{\widehat{G}}_{1} and G^2{\widehat{G}}_{2} acts m−m-transitively on XX for any m∈𝐍.m\in{\bf N}.

While a general hypersurface X⊂𝐂k+2X\subset{\bf C}^{k+2} as above has quite a rich topology, in sections 4 and 6 we give a series of examples of hypersurfaces of this type which are diffeomorphic to the affine space 𝐂k+1,k≥3.{\bf C}^{k+1},\,\,k\geq 3. Presumably, they are not, in general, isomorphic to 𝐂k+1,{\bf C}^{k+1}, and so, they should present new exotic algebraic structures on 𝐂k+1{\bf C}^{k+1} (see e.g. [Za 2]). As well, this would show that the Miyanishi’s characterization of the affine 3-space 𝐀3{\bf A}^{3} [Miy] cannot be applied to 𝐀n{\bf A}^{n} for n≥4n\geq 4 (see Remark 4). But if one of them were isomorphic to 𝐂k+1{\bf C}^{k+1} this would answer in negative alternatively, either to the Zariski Cancellation Problem or to the Abhyankar-Sathaye Embedding Problem (see below).

Sections 1-3 are devoted to a kind of modification which acts on the affine rings producing new affine rings; we call it affine modification. It appeared in passing in the classical Zariski paper [Zar] (see also [Hiro, III.2]), but apparently, the first proper study of this transform was done in [Da]. A geometric counterpart of the affine modification occurred to be useful in constructing exotic algebraic structures on the affine spaces, as it was done in [Ka 1] (see also [Za 2]).

In Corollary 2 we lift automorphisms to an affine modification. In section 3 we provide certain conditions (more general then those in [Ka 1]) which guarantee preservation of the topology under a modification.

Recall the Abhyankar-Sathaye Embedding Problem:

Is every closed embedding of 𝐂k{\bf C}^{k} into 𝐂n{\bf C}^{n} rectifiable, i.e. equivalent to a linear one up to the actions of the automorphisms groups Aut𝐂k\,{\bf C}^{k} resp. Aut𝐂n​?\,{\bf C}^{n}?

In section 7 we give a generalization of the Sathaye-Wright Theorem [Sat, Wr 2] which guarantees rectifiability of the special embeddings 𝐂2↪𝐂3{\bf C}^{2}\hookrightarrow{\bf C}^{3} given by the equations of the form f⁡(x,y)​zn+g⁡(x,y)=0.f(x,\,y)z^{n}+g(x,\,y)=0. Notice that for n=1n=1 such a surface is an affine modification of the affine plane 𝐂2{\bf C}^{2} along the divisor Df=(f)D_{f}=(f) with center at the ideal I=(f,g)⊂𝐂⁡[x,y].I=(f,\,g)\subset{\bf C}[x,\,y]. More generally, in Theorem 7 we show that any smooth acyclic surface X⊂𝐂3X\subset{\bf C}^{3} given by the equation f⁡(x,y)​zn+g⁡(x,y)=0f(x,\,y)z^{n}+g(x,\,y)=0 is isomorphic to 𝐂2{\bf C}^{2} (and can be rectified). This is no longer true for 𝐐−{\bf Q}-acyclic surfaces; see Example 7.

It is well known (see e.g. [Ha, 7.17]) that every birational projective morphism of quasiprojective varieties Y→XY\to X is a blow up of XX with center at a subsheaf of ideals ℐ⊂𝒪X.{\cal I}\subset{\cal O}_{X}. Similarly, we have the following theorem.

Any birational morphism q:Y→Xq\,:\,Y\to X of affine varieties is an affine modification. for some ai,fi∈Aa_{i},\,f_{i}\in A where f=f1⋅…⋅fk∈A,bi=f​ai/fi∈Af=f_{1}\cdot\dots\cdot f_{k}\in A,\,\,b_{i}=fa_{i}/f_{i}\in A and I=(f,b1,…,bk)⊂A,I=(f,\,b_{1},\dots,b_{k})\subset A, as desired. □\Box

2 The universal property of affine modifications

Here we show that the universal property of the blow ups (see e.g. [Hiro]) is still valid for the affine modifications.

3 Topology of affine modifications

In this section we appropriate the complex analytic point of view. Observe that, with the language of schemes, one can naturally extend the notion of the affine modification to quasiprojective varieties and to more general ring spaces and obtain results analogous to those of the previous sections. Instead, to simplify things, according to Proposition 1(a) and Theorem 1 we adopt the following definitions.

Definition 3.1. Consider a triple (M,C,D)(M,\,C,\,D) resp. a pair (M′,E′)(M^{\prime},\,E^{\prime}) where MM resp. M′M^{\prime} is a reduced connected complex space, D⊂MD\subset M resp. E′⊂M′E^{\prime}\subset M^{\prime} is a closed hypersurface, and C⊂DC\subset D is a closed analytic subvariety of codimension at least two in M.M. Let σ:M′→M{\sigma}\,:\,M^{\prime}\to M be a surjective morphism such that the restriction σ|(M′∖E′):M′∖E′→M∖D{\sigma}\,|\,(M^{\prime}\setminus E^{\prime})\,:\,M^{\prime}\setminus E^{\prime}\to M\setminus D is a biholomorphism, and σ⁡(E′)⊂C.{\sigma}(E^{\prime})\subset C. Then we say that the pair (M′,E′)(M^{\prime},\,E^{\prime}) is a pseudoaffine modification (via σ{\sigma}) of the triple (M,C,D)(M,\,C,\,D) with a locus subordinated to (C,D)(C,\,D) and with the exceptional divisor E′.E^{\prime}.

In particular, we consider the pseudoaffine modification M′=ΣC,D​(M)M^{\prime}=\Sigma_{C,\,D}(M) of MM along DD with center C,C, where M′=M^∖D′,M^M^{\prime}={\widehat{M}}\setminus D^{\prime},\,\,\,{\widehat{M}} is the blow up of MM at CC and D′D^{\prime} is the strict transform of DD in M^.{\widehat{M}}.

Anyhow, modifying MM we replace the divisor DD by the new one E′.E^{\prime}. In the latter case E′=E∖D′E^{\prime}=E\setminus D^{\prime} where E=σC−1​(C)⊂M^E={\sigma}_{C}^{-1}(C)\subset{\widehat{M}} is the exceptional divisor of the blow up σC:M^→M\sigma_{C}\,:\,{\widehat{M}}\to M with center C.C. While in the former case we blow up MM with center being an ideal sheaf supported by C.C.

The next theorem and its corollary generalize Theorem 3.5 in [Ka 1] (see also [Za 2, Thm. 5.1]).

Remarks

3.1. If σ=σC{\sigma}={\sigma}_{C} is the blowup morphism with a smooth center CC contained in regD,\,D, or otherwise, if M′M^{\prime} is the affine modification ΣI,f​(M)\Sigma_{I,\,f}(M) with the ideal II admitting a regular system of generators started with ff (see Proposition 1(d)), then τ:E′→C\tau\,:\,E^{\prime}\to C is a smooth fibration over CC with a fibre 𝐂k,{\bf C}^{k}, where k=k=codimCD,{}_{D}C, and so, the contraction σ|E′:E′→C{\sigma}\,|\,E^{\prime}\,:\,E^{\prime}\to C is a homotopy equivalence. Corollary 3.1: Preserving contractibility under a modification.

Suppose that the conditions (ii), (i​iii) and (i​i​iiii) of Theorem 3 are fulfilled. Then the pseudoaffine modification M′M^{\prime} of MM is acyclic resp. contractible iff MM is.

Proof.  The equivalence of acyclicity of M′M^{\prime} and of MM follows immediately from Theorem 3.

By the Hurewicz and Whitehead Theorems [FoFu, (2.11.5), (2.14.2)], contractibility of MM resp. M′M^{\prime} is equivalent to acyclicity and simply connectedness of MM resp. M′.M^{\prime}. Notice that the conditions (ii), (i​i​iiii) and (δ\delta) of Proposition 3 are fulfilled. By (b) of this proposition, σ:M′→M{\sigma}\,:\,M^{\prime}\to M induces an isomorphism of the fundamental groups. Thus, M′M^{\prime} is simply connected iff MM is, and the statement follows. □\Box

Remark 4.3. Presumably, even being diffeomorphic to the affine space, the variety X=X⁡(p1,…,pm)X=X(p_{1},\dots,p_{m}) is not, in general, isomorphic to 𝐂k+1{\bf C}^{k+1} for k≥3,k\geq 3, and so, it should provide an exotic algebraic structure on 𝐂k+1{\bf C}^{k+1} (see e.g. [Za 2]). But at present we have no invariant available to distinguish XX from the affine space (see Remark 5 below).

Suppose that, indeed, for a certain smooth acyclic complete intersection X0⊂𝐂kX_{0}\subset{\bf C}^{k} the variety X=X⁡(p1,…,pm)X=X(p_{1},\dots,p_{m}) is not isomorphic to 𝐂k+1.{\bf C}^{k+1}. Then we would have an example showing that Miyanishi’s characterization of the affine 3-space 𝐀k3{\bf A}^{3}_{k} [Miy] does not hold any more in higher dimensions. Indeed, by Proposition 4, the varieties XX and U0≃X0×𝐂mU_{0}\simeq X_{0}\times{\bf C}^{m} being smooth and acyclic we have e⁡(X)=e⁡(U0)=1,X∖U0≃𝐂∗×𝐂k,e(X)=e(U_{0})=1,\,\,\,X\setminus U_{0}\simeq{\bf C}^{*}\times{\bf C}^{k}, the algebras 𝐂⁡[X]{\bf C}[X] and 𝐂⁡[U0]{\bf C}[U_{0}] are UFD and have only constants as the units (see e.g. [Ka 1, Prop. 3.2]). Further, if for a certain codimension mm smooth acyclic complete intersection X0⊂𝐂kX_{0}\subset{\bf C}^{k} non-isomorphic to 𝐂k−m{\bf C}^{k-m} the variety XX were isomorphic to 𝐂k+1,{\bf C}^{k+1}, this would answer in negative, alternatively, either to the Zariski Cancellation Problem1111 11 In the particular case when k=3k=3 and X0≃𝐂X_{0}\simeq{\bf C} is a complete intersection given by p1​(x¯)=p2​(x¯)=0p_{1}({\bar{x}})=p_{2}({\bar{x}})=0 in 𝐂3,{\bf C}^{3}, the smooth contractible 4-folds X=X⁡(p1,p2)⊂𝐂5X=X(p_{1},\,p_{2})\subset{\bf C}^{5} were studied, in algebraic fashion, in [As] as potential counterexamples to the Zariski Cancellation Problem. Indeed, in [As] an isomorphism X×𝐂≃𝐂5X\times{\bf C}\simeq{\bf C}^{5} was established. or to the Abhyankar-Sathaye Embedding Problem1212 12 Cf. also Remark 6 below for another conjectural counterexample to the Abhyankar-Sathaye Embedding Problem.. Indeed, the former happens if the hypersurface U0=X0×𝐂m⊂XU_{0}=X_{0}\times{\bf C}^{m}\subset X is isomorphic to 𝐂k{\bf C}^{k} (which is only possible if X0X_{0} was contractible). Remarks

6.1. By Corollary 4, the zero fibres of the polynomials u​v−p2, 3​(x,y,z)∈𝐂[5]uv-p_{2,\,3}(x,\,y,\,z)\in{\bf C}^{[5]} and u​v−p2, 30​(x,y,z)∈𝐂[5],uv-p_{2,\,3}^{0}(x,\,y,\,z)\in{\bf C}^{[5]}, as well as the generic fibres of the first one, are smooth contractible hypersurfaces in 𝐂5,{\bf C}^{5}, whereas the generic fibres of the second one have Euler characteristic 55 (see Lemma 4(a)).

6.2. More generally, we have presented above a collection of examples of smooth acyclic hypersurfaces in 𝐂n{\bf C}^{n} (see also [Za 2]). Most of them are not rectifiable; actually, their defining polynomials have a fibre non-isomorphic to 𝐂n−1.{\bf C}^{n-1}. By Corollary 3 (see also Remark 3), performing the affine modification of 𝐂n{\bf C}^{n} along such a hypersurface D=p∗​(0),p∈𝐂[n],D=p^{*}(0),\,\,p\in{\bf C}^{[n]}, with a smooth reduced acyclic center C⊂DC\subset D leads to a smooth contractible affine n−n-fold X.X. The question arises when XX itself is isomorphic to the affine space 𝐂n{\bf C}^{n} (cf. Question A in sect. 7 below).

Suppose that this is the case, and that, moreover, C≃𝐂k.C\simeq{\bf C}^{k}. Then the exceptional divisor E=σC−1​(C)=q∗​(0)⊂XE={\sigma}_{C}^{-1}(C)=q^{*}(0)\subset X where σC:X→𝐂n{\sigma}_{C}\,:\,X\to{\bf C}^{n} is the blowup morphism and q:=p∘σC∈𝐂⁡[X]≃𝐂[n],q:=p\circ{\sigma}_{C}\in{\bf C}[X]\simeq{\bf C}^{[n]}, would be isomorphic to 𝐂n−1.{\bf C}^{n-1}. But qq having a fibre non-isomorphic to 𝐂n−1,{\bf C}^{n-1},\, the hypersurface E≃𝐂n−1E\simeq{\bf C}^{n-1} in X≃𝐂nX\simeq{\bf C}^{n} cannot be rectifiable. Thus, this would answer in negative to the Abhyankar-Sathaye Embedding Problem (cf. Remark 4)1616 16 Recall that the varieties discussed in Remark 4 arise as affine modifications of the affine space 𝐂n{\bf C}^{n} along a hyperplane with non-linear acyclic centers. Whereas here we consider, in particular, affine modifications of 𝐂n{\bf C}^{n} along acyclic hypersurfaces with center at a linear subspace..

7 On the theorems of Sathaye and Wright

We propose the following

Questions

A) When an affine modification X=ΣI,f​(𝐂n)X=\Sigma_{I,\,f}({\bf C}^{n}) of 𝐂n{\bf C}^{n} is isomorphic to 𝐂n​?{\bf C}^{n}?

B) Let X=ΣI,f​(𝐂n)X=\Sigma_{I,\,f}({\bf C}^{n}) be an affine modification of 𝐂n{\bf C}^{n} canonically embedded into 𝐂n+k{\bf C}^{n+k} (see Definition 1). If X≃𝐂n,X\simeq{\bf C}^{n}, is it necessarily rectifiable in 𝐂n+k{\bf C}^{n+k}?

C) Which embeddings 𝐂n↪𝐂n+k{\bf C}^{n}\hookrightarrow{\bf C}^{n+k} appear in this way?

Question B is a specialization of the Abhyankar-Sathaye Embedding Problem mentioned in the Introduction. This problem is known to be answered in affirmative for k≥n+2k\geq n+2 (the Jelonek-Kaliman-Nori-Srinivas Theorem [Je, Ka 2, Sr]) and for n=k=1 (the Abhyankar-Moh and Suzuki Embedding Theorem [AM, Suz]). In a special case when n=2n=2 and k=1k=1 the positive answer to Question B is provided by a theorem of A. Sathaye1717 17 which corresponds to the case n=1n=1 in Theorem 7 below. [Sat], generalized by D. Wright1818 18 See also [Ru 2, RuSat] for some generalizations. [Wr 2] as follows.

Theorem 7.1 (Sathaye–Wright).

Let X=Xn,f,gX=X_{n,\,f,\,g} be a surface in 𝐂3{\bf C}^{3} given by the equation f⁡(x,y)​zn+g⁡(x,y)=0f(x,\,y)z^{n}+g(x,\,y)=0 where f,g∈𝐂⁡[x,y],n∈𝐍.f,\,g\in{\bf C}[x,\,y],\,\,\,n\in{\bf N}. Suppose that X≃𝐂2.X\simeq{\bf C}^{2}. Then XX is rectifiable, i.e. there exists an automorphism α∈\alpha\inAut𝐂2\,{\bf C}^{2} which transforms XX into a coordinate plane.

We give below a new proof of Theorem 7, as well as some generalization. The proof is easy if one of the polynomials f,gf,\,g is constant; in the sequel we do not consider this possibility. Observe that for n=1n=1 the surface X=X1,f,gX=X_{1,\,f,\,g} as in Theorem 7 is the affine modification ΣI,f​(𝐂2)\Sigma_{I,\,f}({\bf C}^{2}) of 𝐂2{\bf C}^{2} along the divisor Df=f∗​(0)D_{f}=f^{*}(0) with center I=(f,g)I=(f,\,g) (see Example 1) whereas the surface Xn,f,gX_{n,\,f,\,g} can be presented as a cyclic covering of X1,f,gX_{1,\,f,\,g} ramified to order nn on Dg=g∗​(0).D_{g}=g^{*}(0). So, in the proof we use affine modifications.

Theorem 7.2. Let X=Xn,f,gX=X_{n,\,f,\,g} be an irreducible smooth surface in 𝐂3{\bf C}^{3} given by the equation f⁡(x,y)​zn+g⁡(x,y)=0f(x,\,y)z^{n}+g(x,\,y)=0 where f,g∈𝐂⁡[x,y],n∈𝐍.f,\,g\in{\bf C}[x,\,y],\,\,n\in{\bf N}. The following conditions (i) - (iv) are equivalent1919 19 Hereafter e⁡(X)e(X) denotes the Euler characteristic of X.X.:

(i) e⁡(X)=1e(X)=1 and H1​(X,𝐙)=0.H_{1}(X;\,{\bf Z})=0.

(ii) XX is acyclic, i.e. H~∗​(X,𝐙)=0.{\tilde{H}}_{*}(X;\,{\bf Z})=0.

(iii) X≃𝐂2.X\simeq{\bf C}^{2}.

(iv) XX is rectifiable.

If n>1,n>1, then the above conditions are equivalent to the following one:

(v) The pair (f,g)(f,\,g) is rectifiable in the following sense: there exists an automorphisms α∈\alpha\inAut𝐂[2]\,{\bf C}^{[2]} such that (α⁡(f),α⁡(g))=(p⁡(x),y).(\alpha(f),\,\alpha(g))=(p(x),\,y).

The implications (v)⟹(i​v)⟹(i​i​i)⟹(i​i)⟹(i)(v)\Longrightarrow(iv)\Longrightarrow(iii)\Longrightarrow(ii)\Longrightarrow(i) are easy; in the sequel we only prove (i)⟹(i​v)(i)\Longrightarrow(iv) in the case n=1n=1 and (i)⟹(v)(i)\Longrightarrow(v) in the case n>1.n>1.

Remarks

7.1. There are examples of acyclic or even contractible smooth algebraic surfaces in 𝐂3{\bf C}^{3} non-isomorphic to 𝐂2,{\bf C}^{2}, see e.g. [tDP, KaML 2] and Example 6 below. Moreover, any smooth contractible affine algebraic surface of logarithmic Kodaira dimension 11 admits such an embedding into 𝐂3{\bf C}^{3} [KaML 2]. However, Theorem 7 shows that the image of this embedding cannot be given by a ‘binomial’ equation f⁡(x,y)​zn+g⁡(x,y)=0.f(x,\,y)z^{n}+g(x,\,y)=0.

7.2. As a corollary we obtain that if the zero fibre of the polynomial f⁡(x,y)​zn+g⁡(x,y)f(x,\,y)z^{n}+g(x,\,y) is acyclic (resp. isomorphic to 𝐂2{\bf C}^{2}) then so is every fibre. Notice that in general, a polynomial p∈𝐂[3]p\in{\bf C}^{[3]} with a smooth acyclic, or even contractible, zero fibre may have non-acyclic generic fibres; see Example 6 above.

7.3. The next simple observation will be useful in what follows. Let X1=X1,f,gX_{1}=X_{1,\,f,\,g} be a surface as in Theorem 7 with n=1.n=1. Since X1X_{1} is supposed being irreducible, the divisors DfD_{f} and DgD_{g} have no irreducible component in common. Thus, the center Df⋅DgD_{f}\cdot D_{g} of the blow up σI:X1→𝐂2,σI​(x,y,z)=(x,y),\sigma_{I}\,:\,X_{1}\to{\bf C}^{2},\,\,\,\sigma_{I}(x,\,y,\,z)=(x,\,y), is supported by the finite set suppDf∩\,D_{f}\capsuppDg\,D_{g} (see Example 1). The exceptional curve E′⊂X1,E′={f(x,y)=g(x,y)=0},E^{\prime}\subset X_{1},\,\,\,E^{\prime}=\{f(x,\,y)=g(x,\,y)=0\}, is isomorphic to the product 𝐂×(CLOSE{\bf C}\times(suppDf∩\,D_{f}\capsuppOPENDg),\,D_{g}), and hence, it consists of κ\kappa vertical lines in X1X_{1} where κ:=\kappa:=card (suppDf∩\,D_{f}\capsuppDg\,D_{g}).

The proof of Theorem 7 is based on the following Lemmas 7 - 7.

Lemma 7.1. Let XX be a smooth irreducible affine surface. Then

(a) The following conditions (ii) and (i​iii) (resp. (i′i^{\prime}) and (i​i′ii^{\prime})) are equivalent:

(ii) e⁡(X)=1e(X)=1 and H1​(X,𝐙)=0H_{1}(X;\,{\bf Z})=0 resp. (i′i^{\prime}) e⁡(X)=1e(X)=1 and b1​(X)=0;b_{1}(X)=0;

(i​iii) XX is acyclic, i.e. H~∗​(X,𝐙)=0,{\tilde{H}}_{*}(X;\,{\bf Z})=0, resp. (i​i′ii^{\prime}) XX is 𝐐−{\bf Q}-acyclic, i.e. H~∗​(X,𝐐)=0.{\tilde{H}}_{*}(X;\,{\bf Q})=0.

(b) If (ii) holds then the algebra A=𝐂⁡[X]A={\bf C}[X] is UFD.

Proof.  (a) The implications (i​iii) ⟹\Longrightarrow (ii) resp. (i​i′ii^{\prime}) ⟹\Longrightarrow (i′i^{\prime}) are straightforward. To prove the converse ones, notice that by the Lefchetz Hyperplane Section Theorem [Mil 1, Thm. 7.2], XX has homotopy type of a finite cell complex of real dimension at most two. Hence, H3​(X,𝐙)=H4​(X,𝐙)=0H_{3}(X;\,{\bf Z})=H_{4}(X;\,{\bf Z})=0 and H2​(X,𝐙)H_{2}(X;\,{\bf Z}) is a free abelian group. Therefore, e⁡(X)=1−b1​(X)+b2​(X),e(X)=1-b_{1}(X)+b_{2}(X), and so, if e⁡(X)=1e(X)=1 and b1​(X)=0,b_{1}(X)=0, then b2​(X)=0,b_{2}(X)=0, and moreover, H2​(X,𝐙)=0.H_{2}(X;\,{\bf Z})=0. Thus, (ii) implies that H~∗​(X,𝐙)=0,{\tilde{H}}_{*}(X;\,{\bf Z})=0, i.e. XX is acyclic; in turn, (i′i^{\prime}) implies that H~∗​(X,𝐐)=0,{\tilde{H}}_{*}(X;\,{\bf Q})=0, i.e. XX is 𝐐−{\bf Q}-acyclic. This proves (a).

In view of (a), (b) follows from [Fuj, (1.17)–(1.20)] (see also [Ka 1, Prop. 3.2]). □\Box

Lemma 7.2. Let f,g∈𝐂[2]∖𝐂f,\,g\in{\bf C}^{[2]}\setminus{\bf C} be two non-constant polynomials without common factor2020 20 For instance, this is so if the surface Xn=Xn,f,gX_{n}=X_{n,\,f,\,g} is irreducible.. Then the surface Xn=Xn,f,g={fzn+g=0}⊂𝐂3X_{n}=X_{n,\,f,\,g}=\{fz^{n}+g=0\}\subset{\bf C}^{3} is smooth iff the following two conditions are fulfilled:

(i) For any point P0∈P_{0}\insuppDf∩\,D_{f}\capsuppDg\,D_{g} the divisor DgD_{g} is non-singular and reduced at P0.P_{0}. If so is the divisor DfD_{f} at P0P_{0} too, then DfD_{f} and DgD_{g} are transversal at P0.P_{0}.

(ii) If n>1,n>1, then DgD_{g} is a smooth reduced divisor.

Proof.  The statement easily follows from the equality

grad​(f​zn−g)=(zn​grad​f−grad​g,n​zn−1​f). □\qquad\qquad\mbox{grad}\,(fz^{n}-g)=(z^{n}\mbox{grad}\,f-\mbox{grad}\,g,\,nz^{n-1}f)\,.\qquad\qquad\qquad\mbox{\hfill$\Box$}

Lemma 7.3. Let XX be a connected complex manifold, and let D1,…,DsD_{1},\dots,D_{s} be reduced irreducible principal divisors in X.X. Set D=⋃i=1sDiD=\bigcup_{i=1}^{s}D_{i} and X∗=X∖D.X^{*}=X\setminus D. Then there is an exact sequence

𝟎⟶𝐙s⟶μH1​(X∗,𝐙)⟶i∗′H1​(X,𝐙)⟶𝟎,{\bf 0}\longrightarrow{\bf Z}^{s}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\mu}}{{\longrightarrow}}H_{1}(X^{*};\,{\bf Z})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i_{*}^{\prime}}}{{\longrightarrow}}H_{1}(X;\,{\bf Z})\longrightarrow{\bf 0}\,\,,

Claim 1. Each irreducible component of DfD_{f} meets suppDg.\,D_{g}.

Claim 5. Df∖DgD_{f}\setminus D_{g} is a smooth divisor. Furthermore, if H1​(X1,𝐙)=0,H_{1}(X_{1};\,{\bf Z})=0, then the divisor DfD_{f} is smooth.

Proof.  Let D=Df(i)D=D_{f}^{(i)} be an irreducible component of the divisor Df.D_{f}. It is simply connected and meets DgD_{g} at a unique point, say, P.P. Let ν:𝐂→D\nu\,:\,{\bf C}\to D be a normalization map such that ν⁡(0)=P.\nu(0)=P. Then the polynomial r:=g∘ν∈𝐂[1]r:=g\circ\nu\in{\bf C}^{[1]} vanishes only at zero. Lemma 7.6. (a) Suppose that the surface XnX_{n} where n>1,n>1, is smooth and irreducible. Then the implication (i)⟹(v)(i)\Longrightarrow(v) of Theorem 7 holds.

(b) Suppose further that the surface X1X_{1} is smooth, irreducible and 𝐐−{\bf Q}-acyclic. Assume also that the curves suppDfD_{f} and suppDgD_{g} meet transversally2121 21 In particular, as follows from Lemma 7(b), suppDfD_{f} is smooth.. Then, by an appropriate automorphism α′=(α,id)∈Aut⁡(𝐂2×𝐂)\alpha^{\prime}=(\alpha,\,{\rm id})\in{\rm Aut}\,({\bf C}^{2}\times{\bf C}) of 𝐂3,{\bf C}^{3}, the equation of XX can be reduced to the following form:

p⁡(x)​z=y+x​h​(x,y)+const.p(x)z=y+xh(x,\,y)+{\rm const}.

Proof.  (a) If the condition (ii) of Theorem 7 is fulfilled then by Lemmas 7(a) and 7(b), both surfaces X1X_{1} and XnX_{n} are acyclic. Thus, by Lemma 7, Dg≃𝐂D_{g}\simeq{\bf C} and Df(i)≃𝐂D_{f}^{(i)}\simeq{\bf C} for each i=1,…,κ.i=1,\dots,\kappa.

Let f1∈𝐂[2]f_{1}\in{\bf C}^{[2]} be an irreducible polynomial which defines the irreducible component Df(1)D_{f}^{(1)} of Df.D_{f}. Since by Lemma 7(b), the components Df(i),i=1,…,κ,D_{f}^{(i)},\,\,i=1,\dots,\kappa, of DfD_{f} are disjoint and simply connected, for each i=1,…,κi=1,\dots,\kappa we have f1|Df(i)≡const=ci,f_{1}\,|\,D_{f}^{(i)}\equiv{\rm const}=c_{i}, and therefore, f=p⁡(f1)f=p(f_{1}) for some polynomial p∈𝐂[1].p\in{\bf C}^{[1]}. In view of Lemma 7(b), the curves Df(1)≃𝐂D_{f}^{(1)}\simeq{\bf C} and Dg≃𝐂D_{g}\simeq{\bf C} meet transversally at a unique point. By the Abhyankar-Moh and Suzuki Embedding Theorem, it follows that α:=(f1,g):𝐂2→𝐂2\alpha:=(f_{1},\,g)\,:\,{\bf C}^{2}\to{\bf C}^{2} is an automorphism which transforms the pair (f1,g)(f_{1},\,g) into a pair of coordinate functions (x,y),(x,\,y), and the pair (f,g)(f,\,g) into the pair (p⁡(x),y),(p(x),\,y), as desired. This proves the implication (ii) ⟹\Longrightarrow (vv) of Theorem 7.

(b) By the Abhyankar-Moh and Suzuki Embedding Theorem, the smooth simply connected curve Df(1)≃𝐂D_{f}^{(1)}\simeq{\bf C} can be transformed into a coordinate line x=0x=0 by an automorphism of 𝐂2.{\bf C}^{2}. Thus, we may assume that f1​(x,y)=x,f_{1}(x,\,y)=x, and so, as above, f⁡(x,y)=p⁡(x)f(x,\,y)=p(x) and X={p(x)z=g(x,y)}⊂𝐂3.X=\{p(x)z=g(x,\,y)\}\subset{\bf C}^{3}.

If xix_{i} is a root of p,p, that is, Df(i)={x=xi},D_{f}^{(i)}=\{x=x_{i}\}, then by Lemma 7(b), the polynomial g⁡(xi,y)∈𝐂⁡[y]g(x_{i},\,y)\in{\bf C}[y] has only one root, say, ci,c_{i}, and this root is simple, that is, g⁡(xi,y)=γi​(y−ci).g(x_{i},\,y)=\gamma_{i}(y-c_{i}). Hence, g⁡(x,y)=γi​(y−ci)+(x−xi)​hi​(x,y)g(x,\,y)=\gamma_{i}(y-c_{i})+(x-x_{i})h_{i}(x,\,y) for a certain hi∈𝐂[2].h_{i}\in{\bf C}^{[2]}. Plugging here x1=0x_{1}=0 and replacing zz by z/γ1,z/\gamma_{1}, we obtain the desired presentation. □\Box

This lemma and the next proposition yield the implication (i)⟹(i​v)(i)\Longrightarrow(iv) of Theorem 7 for n=1.n=1. Denote by GG the subgroup of the group Aut𝐂3\,{\bf C}^{3} which consists of the automorphisms of the type (x,y,z)⟼(x,γ1​y+x​g1,γ2​z+x​g2)(x,\,y,\,z)\longmapsto(x,\,\gamma_{1}y+xg_{1},\,\gamma_{2}z+xg_{2}) where gi∈𝐂[3]g_{i}\in{\bf C}^{[3]} and γi∈𝐂∗,i=1, 2.\gamma_{i}\in{\bf C}^{*},\,\,i=1,\,2.

Proposition 7.1. Let XX be an irreducible smooth 𝐐−{\bf Q}-acyclic surface given in 𝐂3{\bf C}^{3} by the equation p⁡(x)​z=g⁡(x,y)p(x)z=g(x,\,y) where p∈𝐂[1]∖𝐂p\in{\bf C}^{[1]}\setminus{\bf C} and g∈𝐂[2]∖𝐂.g\in{\bf C}^{[2]}\setminus{\bf C}. Suppose that the curves suppDpD_{p} and suppDgD_{g} meet transversally2222 22 By Lemma 7(b), this is true if XX satisfies the condition (ii) of Theorem 7.. Then XX can be transformed into a plane Lc:={y=c},c∈𝐂,L_{c}:=\{y=c\},\,\,c\in{\bf C}, by an automorphism α∈G.\alpha\in G.

The proof proceeds by induction on degp.\,p.

Claim 1. The statement is true if deg​p=1.{\rm deg}\,p=1.

Proof.  We may assume that p⁡(x)=x,p(x)=x, and by Lemma 7(b), that g⁡(x,y)=y+x​h​(x,y)−c,c∈𝐂.g(x,\,y)=y+xh(x,\,y)-c,\,\,c\in{\bf C}. Then the automorphism α∈\alpha\inAut𝐂3,α⁡(x,y,z)=(x,y,z+h),\,{\bf C}^{3},\,\,\,\alpha(x,\,y,\,z)=(x,\,y,\,z+h), transforms XX into the surface X′:={xz=y−c}.X^{\prime}:=\{xz=y-c\}. Furthermore, the automorphism β∈G,β⁡(x,y,z)=(x,y+x​z,z),\beta\in G,\,\,\,\beta(x,\,y,\,z)=(x,\,y+xz,\,z), transforms X′X^{\prime} into the plane Lc.L_{c}. The resulting automorphism α′:=β∘α,\alpha^{\prime}:=\beta\circ\alpha, α′​(x,y,z)=(x,y+x⁡(z+h1),z+h1)\alpha^{\prime}(x,\,y,\,z)=(x,\,y+x(z+h_{1}),\,z+h_{1}) where h1=h⁡(x,y+x​z),h_{1}=h(x,\,y+xz), does not belong, in general, to the group G.G. But composing it further with the automorphism β′∈\beta^{\prime}\inAut𝐂3,β′​(x,y,z)=(x,y,z−h1​(0,y)),\,{\bf C}^{3},\,\,\,\beta^{\prime}(x,\,y,\,z)=(x,\,y,\,z-h_{1}(0,\,y)), we obtain a new one α′′=β′∘α′\alpha^{\prime\prime}=\beta^{\prime}\circ\alpha^{\prime} which does belong to G.G. It remains to note that β′\beta^{\prime} preserves the plane Lc,L_{c}, hence, α′′​(X)=α′​(X)=Lc,\alpha^{\prime\prime}(X)=\alpha^{\prime}(X)=L_{c}, and we are done. □\Box

Claim 2. Let p⁡(x)=x​q​(x)p(x)=xq(x) where deg​q≥1.{\rm deg}\,q\geq 1. Consider the surface Y={q(x)z=g(x,y)}Y=\{q(x)z=g(x,\,y)\} in 𝐂3.{\bf C}^{3}. Then X=ΣI1,ξ​(Y)X=\Sigma_{I_{1},\,\xi}(Y) is the affine modification of YY along the divisor DξD_{\xi} with center I1=(ξ,η)⊂𝐂⁡[Y]I_{1}=(\xi,\,\eta)\subset{\bf C}[Y] where ξ=x|Y\xi=x\,|\,Y and η=z|Y.\eta=z\,|\,Y. Furthermore, YY is a smooth irreducible 𝐐−{\bf Q}-acyclic surface; it is acyclic if XX is.

Proof.  The modification ΣI,x​(𝐂3)\Sigma_{I,\,x}({\bf C}^{3}) along the plane Dx={x=0}D_{x}=\{x=0\} with center I:=(x,z)⊂𝐂[3]I:=(x,\,z)\subset{\bf C}^{[3]} is isomorphic to 𝐂3,{\bf C}^{3}, and the blowup morphism σI:𝐂3→𝐂3{\sigma}_{I}\,:\,{\bf C}^{3}\to{\bf C}^{3} is given as (x,y,z)⟼(x,y,x​z)(x,\,y,\,z)\longmapsto(x,\,y,\,xz) (cf. Examples 1, 2). By Proposition 2(b), the strict transform X=Y′X=Y^{\prime} of YY under σI{\sigma}_{I} coincides with the modification ΣI1,ξ​(Y).\Sigma_{I_{1},\,\xi}(Y). This proves the first assertion.

It is easily seen that under our assumptions, XX being smooth and irreducible implies the same for YY (cf. Lemma 7).

Due to our assumptions and to Lemma 7(b), the irreducible component Dp1:={x=0}D_{p}^{1}:=\{x=0\} of the divisor Dp=p∗​(0)D_{p}=p^{*}(0) in 𝐂2{\bf C}^{2} meets the divisor DgD_{g} transversally at one point, say, P0=(0,y0),P_{0}=(0,\,y_{0}), and DgD_{g} is reduced at P0.P_{0}. Hence, the polynomials x,g⁡(0,y),z∈𝐂[3]x,\,g(0,\,y),\,z\in{\bf C}^{[3]} generate the maximal ideal of the point P0′:=(0,y0, 0)∈Y⊂𝐂3.P_{0}^{\prime}:=(0,\,y_{0},\,0)\in Y\subset{\bf C}^{3}. It follows that I1=(ξ,η)=I⁡(P0′)I_{1}=(\xi,\,\eta)=I(P_{0}^{\prime}) is a maximal ideal of the algebra 𝐂⁡[Y].{\bf C}[Y]. Thereby, the blowup morphism σ:X→Y,σ:=σI1=σI|X,{\sigma}\,:\,X\to Y,\,\,\,{\sigma}:={\sigma}_{I_{1}}={\sigma}_{I}\,|\,X, consists of the usual blow up at P0′P_{0}^{\prime} and deleting the strict transform of the curve l0:={ξ=0}⊂Y,l0≃𝐂,l_{0}:=\{\xi=0\}\subset Y,\,\,l_{0}\simeq{\bf C}, passing through P0′P_{0}^{\prime} (see Proposition 1). By Theorem 3 (see also [Ka 1, Thm. 3.5], [Za 2, Thm. 5.1]), this modification preserves the homology, i.e. σ∗:H∗​(X,𝐙)⟶H∗​(Y,𝐙){\sigma}_{*}\,:\,H_{*}(X;\,{\bf Z})\longrightarrow H_{*}(Y;\,{\bf Z}) is an isomorphism. Claim 3: The induction step. Let YY be as in Claim 2. Suppose that YY can be transformed into a plane Lc:={y=c},c∈𝐂,L_{c}:=\{y=c\},\,\,c\in{\bf C}, by an automorphism α∈G.\alpha\in G. Then the same is true for X.X.

Proof.  Notice that the action of the group GG on 𝐂[3]{\bf C}^{[3]} preserves the ideal I=(x,z)I=(x,\,z) and fixes the element x∈I.x\in I. Therefore, by Corollary 2, α\alpha can be lifted in a unique way to an automorphism α′\alpha^{\prime} of 𝐂3=ΣI,x​(𝐂3){\bf C}^{3}=\Sigma_{I,\,x}({\bf C}^{3}) such that α∘σI=σI∘α′.\alpha\circ{\sigma}_{I}={\sigma}_{I}\circ\alpha^{\prime}. The automorphism α′\alpha^{\prime} is of the form

α′:(x,y,z)⟼(x,γ1​y+x​g1​(x,y,x​z),γ2​z+g2​(x,y,x​z))\alpha^{\prime}\,:\,(x,\,y,\,z)\longmapsto(x,\,\gamma_{1}y+xg_{1}(x,\,y,\,xz),\,\gamma_{2}z+g_{2}(x,\,y,\,xz))

(see Example 2). It sends the surface X=Y′X=Y^{\prime} onto the strict transform Lc′=LcL_{c}^{\prime}=L_{c} of the plane Lc,L_{c}, i.e. again onto the plane LcL_{c} (indeed, σI∗​(y)=y{\sigma}_{I}^{*}(y)=y). Now, composing α′\alpha^{\prime} with the automorphism β∈\beta\inAut𝐂3,β⁡(x,y,z)=(x,y,z−g2​(0,γ1−1​y, 0)),\,{\bf C}^{3},\,\,\,\beta(x,\,y,\,z)=(x,\,y,\,z-g_{2}(0,\,\gamma_{1}^{-1}y,\,0)), we get an automorphism α′′:=β∘α′\alpha^{\prime\prime}:=\beta\circ\alpha^{\prime} which, as it can be easily seen, belongs to the group G.G. Since β\beta preserves the plane Lc,L_{c}, α′′\alpha^{\prime\prime} still transforms XX into this plane. This proves Claim 3 and completes the proof of the proposition. □\Box

Now the proof of Theorem 7 is completed. The next example shows that Theorem 7 cannot be extended to 𝐐−{\bf Q}-acyclic surfaces.

Example 7.1: A Q-acyclic modification of the plane. Consider the surface X⊂𝐂3X\subset{\bf C}^{3} given by the equation x2​z=x+y2.x^{2}z=x+y^{2}. Thus, the assumption of Proposition 7 that the curves suppDpD_{p} and suppDgD_{g} meet transversally is essential, as well as the condition E′=σ∗​(D)E^{\prime}={\sigma}^{*}(D) in (i) of Theorem 3.
